MicroRNA (miRNA) biogenesis and mitochondrial translocation in cardiac cells

Overview of microRNA (miRNA) biogenesis and mitochondrial translocation in cardiac cells. The figure illustrates the canonical pathway of miRNA biogenesis and subsequent mitochondrial import mechanisms relevant to cardiovascular regulation. miRNA transcription is initiated in the nucleus by RNA polymerase II (POL II), generating primary miRNAs (pri-miRNAs), which are processed by the Microprocessor complex (Drosha/DGCR8) into precursor miRNAs (pre-miRNAs). One strand, selected based on thermodynamic stability, is incorporated into the Argonaute-2 (AGO2) protein. AGO2, which may undergo post-translational modifications (PTMs) including phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and malonylation, directs the fate of the miRNA. Depending on cellular context and AGO2 state, the loaded miRNA may exert its function in the cytoplasm, translocate to processing bodies (P-bodies), or be targeted to mitochondria. Mitochondrial translocation occurs through two primary pathways. In the first, the AGO2-miRNA complex is imported via the translocase of the outer membrane (TOM complex, comprising TOM20 and TOM40) and subsequently through the translocase of the inner membrane (TIM complex, including TIM22 or TIM23). In the second mechanism, miRNAs are translocated into the mitochondrial matrix through polynucleotide phosphorylase (PNPase), located at the inner mitochondrial membrane
